19.3.0 (September 9, 2026)

Below is a list of all new features, APIs, and bug fixes.

Read the React 19.3 release post for more information.

  • Fragment Refs: Add Refs to <Fragment /> to support composable platform behavior (@​jackpope, @​sebmarkbage, @​eps1lon, @​Dhakshin2007, @​chirokas, @​teamleaderleo, @​fallintoplace: #32465, #32613, #32619, #32654, #32660, #32682, #32722, #32813, #32814, #33056, #33058, #33093, #34069, #34103, #34544, #34545, #37062, #37061, #37060, #36047, #36010, #35642, #35641, #35637, #35630, #34935, #37457, #37408, #37326, #37251, #37171, #37169, #37168, #37167, #37166, #37165, #37164, #37163, #37162, #37161, #37160, #37125, #37063)

New React DOM Features

  • browser(): a new react-dom API that returns a usable which errors during server rendering and resolves in the browser. use(browser()) inside a <Suspense> boundary marks a subtree as browser-only without reporting a recoverable error (@​gnoff: #37143, #37241)
    • Added an onBrowserBailout option to the react-dom/server APIs to observe when a subtree defers to the browser (@​gnoff #37193)

Notable changes

  • Enable Trusted Types API integration (@​rickhanlonii #35816)
  • Transitions now render independently instead of being entangled into a single render, so a slow transition no longer holds up unrelated ones (@​acdlite #37290)
  • Added a DEV-only warning when a component appears to have been unblocked by calling use() conditionally (@​hoxyq, @​eps1lon: #37104, #37203, #37491)

All Changes

React

  • Fast Refresh Fixes
    • Fix Fast Refresh to find and remount edits to components wrapped behind lazy() (@​sophiebits #36965)
    • Fix Fast Refresh so edits to a memo() comparison function take effect (@​sophiebits #36964)
    • Fix Fast Refresh crash when an edit changes the kind of a component's type (@​sophiebits #36963)
    • Unify hot reload type resolution for Fast Refresh (@​sophiebits #36962)
    • Fix Fast Refresh to remount correctly when an edit changes the component kind (@​sophiebits #36950)
    • Double invoke effects in StrictMode after Fast Refresh (@​eps1lon #35962)
  • Performance Track Fixes
    • Prevent crash when accessing $$typeof in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #35679)
    • Handle non-string function names in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #35659)
    • Use minus (-) instead of en dash for removed props in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #35649)
    • Handle arrays with bigints in deep objects in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #35648)
    • Don't enumerate typed array props in Performance Tracks in DEV (@​UditDewan #36913)
    • Bail out of diffing wide objects and arrays in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #34742)
    • Clear potentially large performance measures in DEV (@​hoxyq #34803)
    • Fix missing else branch for renders with no props change in Performance Tracks (@​hoxyq #34837)
  • Activity Fixes
    • Fix useSyncExternalStore missing store mutations that happened while an Activity tree was hidden (@​sophiebits #36947)
    • Hide portal contents when an Activity is hidden (@​acdlite #35091)
    • Prevent metadata hoisting in hidden <Activity> trees (@​ronnakamoto #34983)
    • Prevent errors thrown inside a hidden Activity from escaping to the visible UI (@​acdlite #35074)
    • Don't unhide a node if a direct parent Offscreen is still hidden (@​sebmarkbage #34821)
    • Don't show internal <Offscreen> component in error messages (@​rickhanlonii #35763)
  • Warn in DEV when a component appears to have been unblocked by a conditional use() (@​hoxyq, @​eps1lon: #37104, #37203, #37491)
  • Render transitions independently instead of entangling them into a single render (@​acdlite #37290)

issue.title: M1: GitHub client, API budget tracking and sync

repository.name: IssueRadar
repository.description: 🔎 Discover unclaimed open-source issues and track your PRs with a daily GitHub digest.

issue.body:
This is the second milestone. IssueRadar can now actually talk to GitHub: you pick repos to watch, run a sync, and it stores their open issues and open PRs locally. Scoring and the daily digest come next.

What I did:

- Wrote the GitHub client. It's the only part of the code that talks to GitHub, and it can only read. Anything that isn't a GET, or a GraphQL query that isn't read-only, gets refused before a request is even built. There are tests for this so it can't quietly change later.
- Added budget tracking. Every response tells me how much of the rate limit is left, so I keep track of it and stop before running out instead of hitting the wall. Sync prints how many requests it used at the end.
- Followed GitHub's own rules for rate limits: wait for `retry-after` if they send it, otherwise wait at least a minute, back off, and give up after a few tries.
- Added ETag caching, so if nothing changed GitHub answers with a 304 and it doesn't cost anything. On my own repo the second sync used no budget at all.
- Set up the database (SQLite) with all the tables from the plan. Migrations run on their own, so there's nothing to set up by hand.
- New commands: `firstpr watch add / remove / list`, `firstpr sync`, and `firstpr doctor --measure-etag owner/repo`.
- Made sync resilient. If one repo fails, the rest still sync. If the rate limit runs out halfway, the next `sync` picks up where it stopped instead of starting over.
- Tests never touch the network. They run against real responses I recorded from this repo, plus GitHub's own documented examples.

Things I found along the way:

- The "open issues" endpoint also returns PRs. On this repo, all 11 "open issues" were actually Dependabot PRs, so I filter those out.
- My plan was to look for `#123` in PR descriptions to spot issues someone is already working on. On real Dependabot PRs that found up to 159 random issue numbers per PR, because they paste in release notes from other projects. So now "fixes #12" counts as a strong link, a plain mention counts as a weak one, and I skip bot PR descriptions completely. The details are in `RESULTS.md` and ADR 0013.
- I also stopped Dependabot from suggesting React 19, since I'm staying on React 18 for now. PRs #12 and #13 can be closed.

To try it:

```powershell
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
$env:FIRSTPR_GITHUB_TOKEN = "your-read-only-token"
firstpr doctor
firstpr watch add modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk
firstpr sync
firstpr sync
```

The second `sync` should come back almost entirely as 304s.

Still to do with my own token: run the ETag check and a sync of around 25 repos, and add the numbers to `RESULTS.md`.

issue.title: M2: scoring engines, explain and evaluation

repository.name: IssueRadar
repository.description: 🔎 Discover unclaimed open-source issues and track your PRs with a daily GitHub digest.

issue.body:
This is the third milestone, and it's the part that actually answers the questions IssueRadar exists for: is this issue free, is it the right level for me, and will anyone review my PR. Every answer comes with the reasons behind it.

What I did:

- Built the "is it free?" check. It looks at assignees, linked PRs (GitHub's linked-PR search, "fixes #12" in open PRs, and the issue timeline), and comments like "can I work on this". If someone claimed it more than 14 days ago with no PR since, it shows as "likely free" with the age. A maintainer saying "feel free to take this" counts as an invitation, not a claim, and there are tests for exactly that.
- Built the difficulty check. Each issue gets a score from 0 to 100, a level (Beginner, Intermediate, Pro), a rough time estimate and a type (docs, tests, bug, and so on). It starts from the labels and adjusts for things like a missing repro, a long discussion, or "needs a proposal first".
- Built repo health: how fast maintainers reply, how many outside PRs get merged, how recently someone pushed, how many PRs are waiting, and whether there's a CONTRIBUTING file and templates. It also flags things to know before starting: a CLA, DCO sign-off, an AI policy, or "open an issue first".
- Added stack matching against my `skills.yaml`, and the ranking that combines everything.
- Sync now reads comments and timelines, but only for the most promising open issues in each repo, so it doesn't burn through the rate limit.
- New commands: `firstpr explain <issue-url>`, `firstpr find` with filters, `firstpr eval sample` and `firstpr eval run`, and `firstpr pack list / add / verify`.
- Wrote `docs/scoring.md`, which explains exactly how every number is calculated.

Things I found along the way:

- GitHub's community profile said my repo has no issue template, even though it has issue forms. It turns out it doesn't count the YAML forms, so I check the folder myself now.
- Upgrading an existing database was quietly deleting rows. SQLite rebuilds tables during a migration, and with foreign keys on that cascades deletes. I turn them off while migrating, and there's a test that would catch it.

What's still open:

- No precision/recall numbers yet. They need issues labelled by hand, so I left `RESULTS.md` saying "not measured yet" instead of putting in numbers I can't back up. The commands and steps are in `eval/README.md`.
- The starter packs aren't verified yet. `firstpr pack verify <name>` checks each repo with my token.

To try it:

```powershell
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
Copy-Item examples\skills.yaml skills.yaml
firstpr pack add ai-agents-and-mcp
firstpr sync
firstpr find --level beginner
firstpr explain https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/issues/1
```
